newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian shares buoyant, seen powering on.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian shares buoyant, seen powering on.

text.p: Renewed buying of oil marketing and bank shares took Nigerian stocks to new heights on Friday and dealers said they expected the trend to continue.
The all-share index was 7182.42 from 7157.52 on Thursday.
Oil shares, the toast of the market, surged despite a fuel scarcity in the commercial hub of Lagos, traders said.
"The shortage arose over a new lifting arrangement. It has nothing to do with the marketers," one trader said, adding that "Demand for the shares does not appear to be waning."
Unipetrol remained the most costly stock, rising one naira to 65.84 naira, the same as Mobil which ended at 54.75 naira.
Improved public perception of banks saw them soar with United Bank for Africa three kobo higher at 7.30 naira on news that it had a new chief executive officer and chairman.

However, FSB International Bank and Union Bank were the sector's biggest beneficiaries, gaining the maximum five percent or 15 kobo and 35 kobo, respectively, to close at 6.40 naira and 7.45 naira while First Bank closed 30 kobo up at 8.45 naira.
Cement shares ended mixed. West African Portland Cement rose by 50 kobo to 51.00 naira while Ashaka Cement fell 30 kobo to 14.50 naira and Benue Cement slumped five kobo to 6.85 naira.
Lever Brothers shed 75 kobo to 17.00 naira as investors continued to off offload its stock.
Paper firm Thomas Wyatt lost 20 kobo to 5.60 naira.

But food companies were up on demand. Nestle closed 20 kobo higher at 53.80 naira, Coca-Cola bottlers Nigerian Bottling Company was 34.00 naira, 30 kobo stronger and Union Dicon Salt ended 22 kobo better at 44.66 naira.
Improved full year result favoured Industrial Gases, which rose 15 kobo to 12.70 naira while Vitafoam notched 10 kobo to 3.90 naira.
Traders said the bullish trend would persist in the weeks ahead, particularly in the active oil, food and banking sectors.
"Unless there is a round of terribly poor results, the oil shares should remain strong," said one.
